# Supabase: Postgres as a backend

[Supabase](https://supabase.com) is a hosted Postgres with a few services around it: an API, Auth,
Edge Functions, Storage and Realtime. Most of what an application needs from a backend is built
from Postgres features. The API is generated from the schema, access control is **Row Level
Security**, and the queue, the scheduler and the secrets are extensions. The database even calls
out to functions over HTTP. The examples come from a small project outside this repository that
syncs Obsidian notes into Supabase for search, run on the Supabase CLI's local stack (Postgres
17.11).

## The API from the schema

[PostgREST](https://postgrest.org) turns the schema into a REST API. Each table and view in an
exposed schema becomes an endpoint under `/rest/v1/`, and each SQL function becomes an RPC endpoint,
so the search function below is called as `POST /rest/v1/rpc/match_user_notes`. The client
libraries wrap these calls, as in the Obsidian plugin:

```ts
const { data, error } = await db.rpc("match_user_notes", { query_embedding, match_count: 8, query_text });
```

The project has no API server of its own. New endpoints come from migrations, and functions that
should stay private live in a schema that PostgREST does not expose, such as `util`.

## Roles and Row Level Security

PostgREST connects to Postgres as the `authenticator` role and switches, for each request, to the
role named in the request's JWT. A publishable key carries `anon`, a signed-in user's token carries
`authenticated`, and a secret key carries `service_role`, which bypasses RLS and belongs only in
server code. The token's claims are set as `request.jwt.claims`, and `auth.uid()` reads the user id
from them, so a policy can compare it with a column:

```sql
alter table public.user_notes enable row level security;

create policy "read own notes"
    on public.user_notes for select
    to authenticated
    using ((select auth.uid()) = user_id);
```

Wrapping `auth.uid()` in a subquery makes Postgres evaluate it once per query instead of once per row.
With the claims set by hand in a transaction, the owner of three notes saw all three, another
signed-in user saw none, and `anon` saw none. The roles also carry their own limits: on the local
stack `anon` has a `statement_timeout` of 3 s and `authenticated` one of 8 s.

Functions run as their caller by default (`security invoker`), so RLS applies inside them, and
`match_user_notes` returns only the caller's rows. A `security definer` function runs as its owner
and bypasses RLS, which the queue triggers below need because the writing user has no rights on the
queue. Each of those functions sets `search_path = ''` and names every object with its schema, so
that a caller cannot redirect it to objects of their own.

## UPDATE without WHERE

The `authenticator` role preloads two libraries, `supautils` and `safeupdate`. **safeupdate**
rejects an `UPDATE` or `DELETE` that has no `WHERE` clause with `UPDATE requires a WHERE clause`.
It applies to every request that comes through the API, including statements inside a `security
definer` function called over RPC, while the same statement run as `postgres` from psql succeeds.
In the project, a function that reset a single-row state table with
`update util.embedding_worker set dispatched_at = '-infinity'` failed only when the Edge Function
called it, and the fix was a `WHERE` clause that matches the one row:

```sql
update util.embedding_worker set dispatched_at = '-infinity' where id;
```

## Queue, schedule and secrets

The project embeds each note section automatically. Inserting a section, or changing its text,
fires a trigger that sends a job to a [pgmq](pgmq.qmd) queue. A dispatcher function then reads a
batch of jobs, takes the Edge Function's URL and an API key from **Vault**, and posts the batch with
**pg_net**:

```sql
select decrypted_secret into api_key
from vault.decrypted_secrets where name = 'embed_cron_key';

perform net.http_post(
    url := function_url,
    body := jsonb_build_object('jobs', batch),
    headers := jsonb_build_object('Content-Type', 'application/json', 'apikey', api_key),
    timeout_milliseconds := 60000
);
```

Vault stores each secret encrypted in `vault.secrets` and decrypts it only in the
`vault.decrypted_secrets` view. `net.http_post` inserts the request into `net.http_request_queue`,
and a background worker sends it after the transaction commits, so the write is not slowed down and
a rolled-back write sends nothing. The Edge Function embeds the batch with gte-small, stores each
vector and deletes its job in one transaction, and then asks the database for the next batch.
**pg_cron** runs the dispatcher at the top of every hour to retry jobs whose request failed:

```sql
select cron.schedule('process-embedding-jobs', '0 * * * *', 'select util.dispatch_embedding_batch()');
```

The dispatcher used to send several batches in parallel. Edge Functions have 2 s of CPU time per
request, and parallel batches of ten long sections ran past it and were cancelled with 503 errors.
The dispatcher now keeps one batch in flight. A single-row table records when the last batch was
sent, and an `UPDATE` on that row, which only one transaction can hold at a time, decides whether a
writer starts a new chain.

The same idea serves the project's Telegram inbox. Two desktops can pull messages without
duplicates, because `update ... set pulled_at = now() where pulled_at is null returning *` marks and
returns each message in one statement.

## Hybrid search

Vector search misses exact names, acronyms and rare words, which full-text search finds.
`match_user_notes` runs both in one SQL function and merges the two rankings by reciprocal rank
fusion. Each section scores `1 / (50 + rank)` in each list it appears in, so a section near the top
of either list ranks high, and highest when it tops both. The lexemes live in a stored generated
column, with the file name and heading weighted above the text:

```sql
alter table public.user_notes
    add column fts tsvector generated always as (
        setweight(
            to_tsvector(
                'english',
                regexp_replace(coalesce(source_path, ''), '^.*/|\.md$', '', 'g') || ' ' || coalesce(heading, '')
            ),
            'A'
        )
        || setweight(to_tsvector('english', body), 'B')
    ) stored;

create index user_notes_fts_idx on public.user_notes using gin (fts);
```

The column names the `english` configuration, because a generated column needs an immutable
expression and the default configuration is a setting that can change.[^magda-gen] The query side
uses `websearch_to_tsquery`, which accepts what a user types, including quoted phrases, `or` and
`-` exclusions, without raising a syntax error, and ranks matches with `ts_rank_cd`, which favors
documents where the query terms appear close together.[^magda-rank] A GIN index stores only the
lexemes and the rows that contain them, without their positions or weights, so Postgres reads those
from the table when it ranks.[^magda-gin] The function also returns snippets made with `ts_headline`,
whose output is not safe to insert into a web page without sanitizing it.[^magda-headline]

## Supabase and AWS

Each Supabase service has a counterpart among AWS services, and Supabase itself runs on AWS:

| Supabase | AWS |
|---|---|
| Postgres | RDS or Aurora |
| PostgREST | API Gateway and the CRUD Lambdas behind it |
| Auth | Cognito |
| Edge Functions | Lambda |
| pgmq | SQS |
| pg_cron | EventBridge Scheduler |
| Vault | Secrets Manager |
| Storage | S3 |
| Realtime | AppSync or WebSocket APIs in API Gateway |

On AWS these are separate services joined by IAM policies. In Supabase the queue, the schedule, the
secrets and the access rules are Postgres objects, created by migrations and covered by the same
transactions as the data. Edge Functions are closer to Cloudflare Workers than to Lambda: they run
TypeScript, JavaScript or WebAssembly on Deno, with 256 MB of memory and 2 s of CPU per request.

[^magda-gen]: Denis Magda, *Just Use Postgres!* (Manning), chapter 6, p. 50 of the Supabase-curated
  Manning sampler *Mastering PostgreSQL* (2026).
[^magda-rank]: Magda, *Just Use Postgres!*, chapter 6, sampler pp. 57 and 59.
[^magda-gin]: Magda, *Just Use Postgres!*, chapter 6, sampler pp. 70–71, which also names the RUM
  index for queries that need positions from the index.
[^magda-headline]: Magda, *Just Use Postgres!*, chapter 6, sampler p. 67.
